\chapter{Learning Theory — Rademacher}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.LearningTheory.JohnsonLindenstrauss.Rademacher
\section{Overview}

This module establishes the Johnson--Lindenstrauss concentration bound for the
Rademacher (random $\pm 1/\sqrt{k}$) matrix.  It proceeds in two layers: a
distribution-agnostic sub-Gaussian concentration theorem
(\lean{jl\_concentration\_single\_subgaussian}) is proved first, and then the
explicit Rademacher construction is shown to satisfy its hypotheses, yielding the
concrete bound $\Pr[\varepsilon\norm{x}^2 < \abs{\norm{Ax}^2 - \norm{x}^2}] \leq
2\exp(-k\varepsilon^2/8)$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{theorem}[Distribution-agnostic JL single-vector concentration]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_subgaussian}
\leanok
\uses{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF, jl_concentration_single_via_bernstein}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ be a random matrix on a probability
space, and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be a nonzero vector.  Suppose the $k$ row
projections $(Ax)_i$ are mutually independent, each integrable against
$e^{t(\cdot)}$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, each has sub-Gaussian MGF bounded
by $\exp\!\bigl((\norm{x}^2/k)\,t^2/2\bigr)$, and each satisfies
$\int (Ax)_i^2 \, d\mu = \norm{x}^2/k$.  Then for every $0 < \varepsilon < 1$,
\[
  \Pr\!\bigl[\varepsilon\norm{x}^2 < \bigl|\norm{Ax}^2 - \norm{x}^2\bigr|\bigr]
  \;\leq\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{k\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Rademacher distribution on $\mathbb{R}$]
\lean{rademacherReal}
\leanok
The Rademacher distribution $\mathrm{Rad}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is the measure
$\tfrac{1}{2}\delta_{-1} + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta_{+1}$, placing equal mass $1/2$
at $-1$ and at $+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[$1/2$ is finite as an extended non-negative real]
\lean{rad_half_ne_top}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
The value $1/2$, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^\infty$, is not
equal to $\top$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Rademacher support in $[-1,1]$]
\lean{rademacherReal_mem_Icc}
\leanok
\uses{rademacherReal}
\difficulty{3}
Almost every sample from the Rademacher distribution lies in the interval
$[-1, 1]$: $\mathrm{Rad}$-a.e.\ $y \in [-1, 1]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Integrability under a scaled Dirac measure]
\lean{integrable_smul_dirac}
\leanok
\uses{rad_half_ne_top}
\difficulty{1}
For any $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and any measurable function $f : \mathbb{R} \to
\mathbb{R}$, the function $f$ is integrable with respect to the measure
$\tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta_a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Every function is integrable under the Rademacher measure]
\lean{integrable_rademacherReal}
\leanok
\uses{integrable_smul_dirac, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{1}
For any $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the function $f$ is integrable with
respect to the Rademacher measure $\mathrm{Rad}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Mean of the Rademacher distribution is zero]
\lean{integral_id_rademacherReal}
\leanok
\uses{integrable_smul_dirac, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{3}
The expected value of the identity under the Rademacher distribution is zero:
$\int y \, d\mathrm{Rad}(y) = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Second moment of the Rademacher distribution is one]
\lean{integral_sq_rademacherReal}
\leanok
\uses{integrable_smul_dirac, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{3}
The second moment of the Rademacher distribution equals one:
$\int y^2 \, d\mathrm{Rad}(y) = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Identity is sub-Gaussian with parameter $1$ under $\mathrm{Rad}$]
\lean{hasSubgaussianMGF_id_rademacherReal}
\leanok
\uses{integral_id_rademacherReal, rademacherReal, rademacherReal_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{4}
The identity function $\mathrm{id} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{HasSubgaussianMGF}(\mathrm{id}, 1, \mathrm{Rad})$, i.e.\ its MGF is
bounded by $e^{t^2/2}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.  This follows from
Hoeffding's lemma applied to the centred random variable supported in $[-1, 1]$,
whose sub-Gaussian parameter is $\bigl((1-(-1))/2\bigr)^2 = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Rademacher matrix sample space]
\lean{RadΩ}
\leanok
The sample space for the Rademacher matrix is $\mathrm{Fin}\,k \to
\mathrm{Fin}\,d \to \mathbb{R}$, i.e.\ the type of $k \times d$ arrays of
real numbers, indexed by $(i,j) \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k \times \mathrm{Fin}\,d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Joint Rademacher product measure]
\lean{radJointMeasure}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, rademacherReal}
The joint measure on $\mathrm{Rad\Omega}(k,d)$ is the product measure
$\bigotimes_{(i,j)} \mathrm{Rad}$, making all $k \cdot d$ entries i.i.d.\
Rademacher.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rademacher matrix]
\lean{radMatrix}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ}
The Rademacher matrix $A : \mathrm{Rad\Omega}(k,d) \to \mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$
maps a sample $\omega$ to the matrix with entries
$A(\omega)_{ij} = \omega_{ij}/\sqrt{k}$, scaling the raw $\pm 1$ entries by
$1/\sqrt{k}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Measurability of the Rademacher matrix]
\lean{measurable_radMatrix}
\leanok
\uses{radMatrix}
\difficulty{2}
The map $\omega \mapsto \mathrm{radMatrix}(k,d,\omega)$ is measurable with
respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathrm{Rad\Omega}(k,d)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row marginal of the joint measure]
\lean{radJointMeasure_row_marginal}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{1}
The pushforward of the joint measure along the $i$-th row projection
$\omega \mapsto \omega_i$ equals the product measure
$\bigotimes_{j \in \mathrm{Fin}\,d} \mathrm{Rad}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Entry marginal of the joint measure]
\lean{radJointMeasure_entry_marginal}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_row_marginal, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{4}
The pushforward of the joint measure along the $(i,j)$-entry projection
$\omega \mapsto \omega_{ij}$ equals $\mathrm{Rad}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Within-row entries are i.i.d.\ Rademacher]
\lean{radJointMeasure_row_iid}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, radJointMeasure_row_marginal, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{4}
For each fixed row $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$, the $d$ functions
$j \mapsto \omega_{ij}$ are mutually independent under the joint measure.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Rows are mutually independent]
\lean{radJointMeasure_rows_iid}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure}
\difficulty{1}
The $k$ row vectors $i \mapsto (\omega_{ij})_{j}$, viewed as
$\mathrm{Fin}\,d \to \mathbb{R}$-valued random variables, are mutually
independent under the joint measure.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Each entry is sub-Gaussian with parameter $1$]
\lean{hasSubgaussianMGF_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, hasSubgaussianMGF_id_rademacherReal, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{3}
For each $(i,j) \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k \times \mathrm{Fin}\,d$, the function
$\omega \mapsto \omega_{ij}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{HasSubgaussianMGF}(\cdot, 1, \mathrm{radJointMeasure})$ under the
joint product measure.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Scaled entry is sub-Gaussian with parameter $x_j^2/k$]
\lean{hasSubgaussianMGF_scaled_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, integral_id_rademacherReal, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, rademacherReal, rademacherReal_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{6}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and indices $i,j$, the function
$\omega \mapsto (x_j / \sqrt{k})\,\omega_{ij}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{HasSubgaussianMGF}(\cdot, x_j^2/k, \mathrm{radJointMeasure})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row projection is sub-Gaussian with parameter $\norm{x}^2/k$]
\lean{hasSubgaussianMGF_row_proj}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, hasSubgaussianMGF_scaled_entry, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_row_iid, radMatrix}
\difficulty{5}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$, the $i$-th row
projection $\omega \mapsto (A(\omega)\,x)_i = (1/\sqrt{k})\sum_j \omega_{ij} x_j$
satisfies $\mathrm{HasSubgaussianMGF}(\cdot, \norm{x}^2/k,
\mathrm{radJointMeasure})$.  This follows by combining per-summand Hoeffding
bounds with independence of the within-row entries.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Variance of $\mathrm{id}$ under $\mathrm{Rad}$ is $1$]
\lean{variance_id_rademacherReal}
\leanok
\uses{integral_id_rademacherReal, integral_sq_rademacherReal, rademacherReal, rademacherReal_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{4}
The variance of the identity function under the Rademacher distribution is $1$:
$\mathrm{Var}[\mathrm{id}; \mathrm{Rad}] = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Variance of a single entry is $1$]
\lean{variance_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, variance_id_rademacherReal}
\difficulty{3}
For any $(i,j)$, the variance of the entry $\omega \mapsto \omega_{ij}$ under
the joint measure is $1$:
$\mathrm{Var}[\omega \mapsto \omega_{ij}; \mathrm{radJointMeasure}] = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Mean of a single entry is $0$]
\lean{integral_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, integral_id_rademacherReal, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, rademacherReal}
\difficulty{4}
For any $(i,j)$, the expected value of $\omega_{ij}$ under the joint measure is
$0$: $\int \omega_{ij} \, d\mathrm{radJointMeasure} = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Scaled entry belongs to $L^2$]
\lean{memLp_scaled_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_entry_marginal, rademacherReal_mem_Icc}
\difficulty{5}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and indices $i,j$, the function
$\omega \mapsto (x_j/\sqrt{k})\,\omega_{ij}$ belongs to $L^2(\mathrm{radJointMeasure})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Variance of a scaled entry is $x_j^2/k$]
\lean{variance_scaled_entry}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, variance_entry}
\difficulty{4}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and indices $i,j$,
$\mathrm{Var}[\omega \mapsto (x_j/\sqrt{k})\,\omega_{ij}; \mathrm{radJointMeasure}]
= x_j^2/k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Variance of the row projection is $\norm{x}^2/k$]
\lean{variance_row_proj}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, memLp_scaled_entry, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_row_iid, radMatrix, variance_scaled_entry}
\difficulty{5}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$,
\[
  \mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[\omega \mapsto (A(\omega)\,x)_i;\,\mathrm{radJointMeasure}\bigr]
  = \frac{\norm{x}^2}{k}.
\]
This follows from per-summand variance $x_j^2/k$ together with
within-row independence.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Mean of the row projection is $0$]
\lean{integral_row_proj}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, integral_entry, memLp_scaled_entry, radJointMeasure, radMatrix}
\difficulty{4}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$,
$\int (A(\omega)\,x)_i \, d\mathrm{radJointMeasure} = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Second moment of the row projection equals $\norm{x}^2/k$]
\lean{integral_sq_row_proj}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, hasSubgaussianMGF_row_proj, integral_row_proj, memLp_scaled_entry, radJointMeasure, radMatrix, variance_row_proj}
\difficulty{5}
For $k > 0$, $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$,
\[
  \int \bigl((A(\omega)\,x)_i\bigr)^2 \, d\mathrm{radJointMeasure}
  = \frac{\norm{x}^2}{k}.
\]
This follows from $\int Y^2 = \mathrm{Var}[Y] + (\int Y)^2 = \norm{x}^2/k + 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row projections are mutually independent]
\lean{radMatrix_proj_indep}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radJointMeasure, radJointMeasure_rows_iid, radMatrix}
\difficulty{3}
For any $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the $k$ row projections
$i \mapsto (A(\omega)\,x)_i$ are mutually independent random variables under
the joint Rademacher measure.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row projections are measurable]
\lean{radMatrix_proj_meas}
\leanok
\uses{RadΩ, radMatrix}
\difficulty{2}
For any $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,k$, the map
$\omega \mapsto (A(\omega)\,x)_i$ is measurable.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[JL concentration for the Rademacher matrix]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_rademacher}
\leanok
\uses{hasSubgaussianMGF_row_proj, integral_sq_row_proj, jl_concentration_single_subgaussian, radJointMeasure, radMatrix, radMatrix_proj_indep, radMatrix_proj_meas}
\difficulty{4}
Let $k, d \geq 1$ and let $A$ be the Rademacher matrix $\mathrm{radMatrix}(k,d)$
on the joint $\pm 1$ sample space.  For every nonzero $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and
every $0 < \varepsilon < 1$,
\[
  \Pr_{\mathrm{radJointMeasure}}\!\bigl[
    \varepsilon\norm{x}^2 < \bigl|\norm{A\omega\, x}^2 - \norm{x}^2\bigr|
  \bigr]
  \;\leq\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{k\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
This recovers Achlioptas's $\pm 1$-entries variant of Johnson--Lindenstrauss
with the Dasgupta--Gupta exponent.
\end{theorem}
